newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australia wheat could rise above 20 m/t - AWB.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australia wheat could rise above 20 m/t - AWB.

text.p: The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) acknowleged on Tuesday that its latest upgrade may still under-estimate the size of the Australian crop, and it accused Argentina of dumping wheat on already flooded world markets.

The current estimate of a 1996/97 (April/March) Australian wheat crop of about 20 million tonnes may end up being "a bit light on", AWB deputy chairman Rob Barry told a meeting of the New South Wales Farmers' Association.

The comments were the first acknowlegement by the AWB of the market view that the AWB has been under-estimating the 1996/97 wheat crop for months and comes only a week after the AWB upgraded its forecast to 20 million from 19 million.
While accusing Argentina of dumping wheat internationally, Barry said the AWB had sold forward large amounts of wheat at high prices earlier this year and had extremely low stocks.
The AWB's estimated net stock position at December 1 was minus 300,000 tonnes, he said.
Additionally, about 1.5 million tonnes of pool wheat had been sold forward at much higher prices than currently available, Barry said.
About 15 percent of the pool has been hedged using futures at or about the peak of the market, in May. The board had used all of its limits at about the right time, he said.
About 45 percent of its foreign exchange exposure had been hedged at lower cross rates than the current market, he said.
"The (AWB is) pretty pleased with how (it has) been able to handle this particular position," he said.

But on Argentina, Barry said: "What's driving the market is the need for Argentina to sell its wheat and it's dumping its wheat on the market as they don't have the storage facilities ... Argentina is price-setter on international market at present," he said.
Discussing the present international supply and demand balance for wheat, he said: "What could go wrong as far as prices, went wrong, and what could go right as far as crops, went right."
Estimates for Australian 1996/97 production between May and October rose by two million tonnes.

In the same period, estimates for production in Canada rose by one million tonnes, in Argentina by about two million tonnes, in the EU by just under two million tonnes and in the U.S. by six million tonnes. This produced a total increase in world production of almost 13 million tonnes. At the same time, international demand fell by about five million tonnes, he said.
With just over 100 million tonnes of wheat traded in the international market, the changes represented about 17 percent of the market, he said. "It is quite significant."

World end-stocks were expected to increase by 15 million tonnes to 119 million tonnes, causing the stock-to-use ratio to increase from 16 to 17 percent last year to about 20 percent at the end of the present harvest, Barry said.
Responding to questions, Barry said the AWB was positive about longer-term world supply/demand.
The market remained very volatile with the world stock-to-use ratio still very low, he said.
But estimates of demand, particularly from Asia and especially by China, were very positive long-term, he said.
Weather-effects on about 30 percent to 40 percent of the Canadian crop would produce downward pressure on the international market for feed grain, he added.
